title: Tansy and the Wobbly Sprite
markdown:
The trees remember this story. The bees, who are busy, remember the humming part.

The sun was just beginning to yawn, stretching golden fingers across the meadow, when Tansy the fox received her very own broomstick. Not just any broomstick. This one had been whispered about in the rustling reeds. It was called Whirlwind, said to be the fastest, steadiest flyer in all of Sunny Meadow. Tansy's heart did a little flutter-thump. She imagined soaring like a swift, dipping and dancing, fur streaming like a golden banner. She patted the handle, smooth as river stone, polished by a thousand happy breezes.

"Ready for adventure, old friend?"

But when Tansy hopped on, expecting to glide, Whirlwind did a funny little jig. Lurch left. Dip right, like a startled frog into a puddle.

"Whoa there, Whirlwind!"

The broomstick swayed and swirled. Tansy's tummy did flip-flops. It would not fly straight. It felt like balancing on wobbly jelly.

Whirlwind, Whirlwind, dip and sway —
not the flying for today.

Tansy had an excellent nose for trouble and interesting smells. She sniffed the bristles. Moss after a summer shower, and something else: a tiny tinkling tinkle. A faint warm shimmer in the bristly depths.

There, nestled deep in the bristles, was a nest: dandelion fluff, shed robin feathers, shimmering spider silk. Curled asleep, a very tiny creature with wings like delicate glass, rainbow glints. This was Wobble, a broomstick sprite. He had found the bristles to be the perfect springy bed, soft as a cloud, warm as a sunbeam.

"Oh," Tansy gasped, hushed. "You're the reason Whirlwind won't fly straight. You're making him all wobbly."

Then she remembered. Mother had given her a basket of ripe juicy star-berries, sparkling like tiny captured constellations, to deliver to Grandma Willow on the other side of Whispering Woods before the sun dipped. The basket was heavy. The journey was long. Whirlwind was meant to be a golden shortcut. How could she fly straight with a nest making the broom bounce like a runaway tumbleweed? The sun was already descending, shy colours, a warm blush on the clouds. The air grew cooler, damp earth of evening. Tansy's tummy fluttered, dry leaves in a gust.

She nudged the nest. Wobble stirred, bell-like, a sleepy chime. "Who's there?"

"Tansy the fox. You're in my broomstick. I need to deliver these star-berries to Grandma Willow, and the sun is setting. It's very important."

Wobble sat up. Tiny soft lights glowed all around the nest: little glow-worms, curled with him, pulsing like heartbeats. His wings drooped.

"Oh, dear. I didn't mean to make trouble. I found this lovely soft spot. My glow-worm friends needed a safe warm place. Their lights help them stay cozy. I thought Whirlwind's bristles were perfect, like a hug from a giant fluffy dandelion."

He gestured toward the handle. "When the wind blows strong, it can shake their little lights right out. So I make sure the bristles sway a little. A gentle rocking boat, just for them."

That was the turn. Wobble was not being cheeky. He was being kind. His heart was as warm as a hearth. The kindness, all the same, made the berry-run impossible.

"Patience now," Tansy said, softer than a moth's wing. She looked at the star-berries. She looked at the glow-worms. "What if we worked together? They need a gentle sway. The berries need a steady flight. Perhaps Whirlwind can do both."

Wobble's wings fluttered, hopeful butterflies. "Together?"

He thought, tiny brow furrowed. Then his face brightened. "What if I made a slightly larger nest near the handle? Steadier. I could still sway it by humming a special song. And you could fly. And the star-berries would be safe."

So: fluff from the meadow, strong spider silk, careful weaving. A new snug nook that would not make Whirlwind wobble too much. Tansy set the basket close, balanced.

"Ready?" Her paw on the handle.
"Ready!" A happy chime.

She hopped on. This time Whirlwind had a gentle rhythmic sway, smooth, not jerky. Dancing, not tumbling. The basket sat still. The new nest sat still-enough. Wobble hummed a lullaby that was mostly wind and a little bell. Glow-worms pulsed a peaceful beat. Tansy guided with a steady paw. They flew over whispering trees, leaves rustling like secrets. A stream winked. A crow, who had opinions about foxes on brooms, decided not to share them. The sun painted orange and purple, a giant artist's palette. They landed at Grandma Willow's cottage as the last sliver of sun dipped, long sleepy shadows on the step.

Grandma Willow smiled a warm crinkly smile, eyes as kind as moonlight. She took the berries. She did not ask about sprites. She might have seen the little lights anyway; grandmothers often do. She set out a thimble of something sweet for anyone small enough to want it. Wobble did.

Tansy did not tell the trees that the best journeys are with friends. The trees were already nodding, branches swaying, as trees do in evening. Wobble's song went on, a small extra wind in the bristles, and Whirlwind, who had a mind of his own, seemed pleased to have two kinds of passengers, and a third if you counted the glow.
